title: American Cooking
description: Ten stories, letters and reports about American food: gumbo, barbecue, Tex-Mex, clam chowder, apple pie, a diner, a cooking class and the memories food carries.

lessons.title: Mom's Gumbo
lessons.summary: Luke learns to make his family's gumbo, and his mother tells him where the Cajun recipe comes from.
lessons.text:
My name is Luke, and my family lives in a small town in Louisiana. Every Sunday, my mother makes gumbo for the whole family. Gumbo is a thick, dark soup with chicken, meat or fish, and it is always served over white rice. Last winter, when I was home from college, I finally asked Mom to teach me.

"Gumbo isn't hard," Mom said, "but you have to be careful and patient." First, we washed a bunch of green onions and a bunch of fresh herbs, and I cut them into small pieces. Then she showed me the most important step. We put oil and flour into a heavy pan and cooked them together over low heat. I had to keep mixing them for almost an hour, until they turned the color of dark chocolate. "Be careful," Mom said. "If it burns, you have to throw it away and start again." I was very careful, and I didn't stop once.

When the color was perfectly dark, we added the onions, the chicken and some water, and soon the kitchen smelled wonderful. While the gumbo was cooking, Mom told me about our family. We are Cajun. About 270 years ago, the Cajun people lived in a French colony in what is now the Canadian province of Nova Scotia. They were forced to leave that province, and many of them came to Louisiana. There they built small settlements along the rivers. Life in those settlements was hard. The people were mainly farmers and fishermen, and they cooked mainly with what they had: rice, fish, chicken and plants from the land. "A typical Cajun meal was simple," Mom said. "Some rice, a little meat and a lot of flavor. Gumbo is a typical example. My mother learned it from her mother, and I learned it from her."

At 6 o'clock, the family sat down at the big table. Before we ate, my father said grace. Grace is a short prayer before a meal. In his prayer, he thanked God for the food and for the family. Then Mom added her own short prayer: "And thank you for our new cook." Everybody looked at me and smiled.

The gumbo was perfectly thick, and the rice was perfectly soft. If I hadn't asked Mom that winter, I would never have learned the family recipe. Now I make gumbo for my friends at college, and I always serve it over rice, just like her. I only wish I had asked her sooner.

Questions:
What does Luke's mother make every Sunday?
She makes gumbo for the whole family.
What is gumbo always served over?
It is always served over white rice.
Why did Luke have to be careful with the oil and flour?
He had to be careful because, if it burned, they would have to throw it away and start again.
Where did the Cajun people build their settlements?
They built small settlements along the rivers of Louisiana.
What is grace?
Grace is a short prayer before a meal.
What does Luke wish?
He wishes he had asked his mother sooner.

lessons.title: The Blind Taste Test
lessons.summary: Ben enters a barbecue contest for the first time, and the judges choose the best meat in a blind test.
lessons.text:
Every spring, the town of Riverton holds a barbecue contest on the grass of its golf course. It is the premier barbecue event in the state, and cooks come from hundreds of miles away. Many people say it is the premier event of its kind in the whole country. This year, Ben Carter decided to enter for the first time.

Ben had been cooking meat over a slow fire in his backyard for 20 years. Using logs from the old oak trees on his farm, he cooked the meat very slowly, for 12 hours. "The logs give the meat its flavor," he always said. His friends had praised his cooking for years, but he had never cooked for real judges.

The contest was a blind taste test. Each cook put a piece of meat into a plain white box with only a number on it. The judges could not see the names of the cooks, so they didn't know whose meat they were eating. "A blind test is the only fair test," said Linda Moore, the head judge. "In a blind test, only the food matters."

Arriving at the golf course early in the morning, Ben saw 60 other cooks with huge, expensive grills. "I should have brought a bigger grill," he thought. But he lit his fire, put on his logs and waited.

At noon, the judges began their work. Sitting at a long table, they examined each piece of meat carefully. They examined the color, the smell and how soft the meat was. Then they tasted it. They wrote down every score, so they could make a fair comparison at the end. "The comparison is the hardest part," Ms. Moore said later. "Many of the boxes were excellent."

At 5 o'clock, the judges concluded their work, and Ms. Moore stood up. "We have concluded that the best meat today was in box 27," she said. Box 27 was Ben's box. Everyone clapped, and in a flash, a photographer was standing in front of him. The camera's flash went off again and again.

Later, the judges praised the rich flavor of his meat. "You must have used oak logs," one judge said. "We could taste it." Ben smiled. "My friends have praised it for years," he said, "but I never thought real judges would praise it too." Next year, he is going to come back to the golf course with the same old grill.

Questions:
Where is the barbecue contest held?
It is held on the grass of the town's golf course.
What did Ben use to cook his meat?
He used logs from the old oak trees on his farm.
Why was it a blind test?
It was a blind test because the judges could not see the names of the cooks.
What did the judges examine?
They examined the color, the smell and how soft the meat was.
Why did the judges write down every score?
They wrote down every score so they could make a fair comparison at the end.
What did the judges praise?
They praised the rich flavor of his meat.

lessons.title: The Food Truck's Debut
lessons.summary: In an e-mail to her friends, Lucia writes about the first day of her Tex-Mex food truck and her plans.
lessons.text:
Subject: Thank you for coming to our debut!

Hi everyone,

Thank you so much for coming to the debut of our food truck, Lucia's Kitchen, on Saturday! For those of you who missed it, here is some info about how it went and what comes next.

As you know, Carlos and I have been planning this truck for 2 years. We sell Tex-Mex food, which is a mix of Mexican and Texan cooking: rice, beans, grilled chicken and lots of cheese. Our most popular dish is "chips and cheese": warm corn chips covered with melted cheese, tomatoes and green peppers.

The debut was a big success. We parked in our own neighborhood, next to the park on Elm Street, and our neighbors came out in large numbers. As a promotion, we gave free chips to the first 50 customers. The promotion worked even better than we expected. The line was so long that we ran out of chips by noon, and Carlos had to drive to the store to buy more chips and cheese.

Starting a food truck is not cheap. The truck itself was our biggest expense, and the kitchen equipment was the second biggest expense. We also pay for gas, food and insurance every month. Still, we want to keep our prices reasonable. A full plate of chicken, rice and beans costs $9, which we think is reasonable for fresh food made by hand.

We could not have done this without our supporters. My sister painted the truck. Our friend Sam built our website. And all of you, our very first supporters, told your friends and families about us. If you hadn't helped us, the debut would never have been such a success.

Here is the info for the next few weeks. From Monday to Friday, we will be parking outside the hospital at lunchtime. On Saturdays, we will be back in our neighborhood, next to the park. By the end of the summer, we will have visited 6 different neighborhoods around the city. You can find more info and our full menu on our website.

See you soon, and come hungry!

Lucia

Questions:
What kind of food does Lucia's Kitchen sell?
It sells Tex-Mex food, which is a mix of Mexican and Texan cooking.
What was the promotion on the first day?
They gave free chips to the first 50 customers.
Why did Carlos have to drive to the store?
He had to drive to the store because they ran out of chips by noon.
What was their biggest expense?
The truck itself was their biggest expense.
Why does Lucia think $9 is reasonable?
She thinks it is reasonable for fresh food made by hand.
Where will the truck be parking from Monday to Friday?
It will be parking outside the hospital at lunchtime.

lessons.title: The Cooking Class
lessons.summary: Nina takes an evening class at a cooking academy and learns to make Southern fried chicken.
lessons.text:
Nina Park had always wanted to cook better, so in October she signed up for an evening class at the Lakeside Cooking Academy. The academy trains people who want to work in restaurants, but it also offers short educational classes for people who just want to cook at home. Nina's class was called "Southern Cooking," and the first lesson was fried chicken.

The teacher, Daniel Ross, had worked in restaurants for 25 years before he joined the academy. "My job is not only to cook," he told the 12 students. "My job is to educate. I want to educate you so well that you will be capable of making this dish without a recipe." Nina wasn't sure she was capable of that. At home, she usually bought her dinner on the way back from work.

"Please ask questions," Mr. Ross said. "There are no dumb questions in my kitchen." So Nina asked one right away: "Why do we put the chicken in milk?" It didn't feel like a dumb question, and Mr. Ross was happy to explain. The milk makes the meat soft, he said.

First, the students mixed flour, salt and black pepper in a large bowl. Then Mr. Ross showed them the most important instrument for frying: a small kitchen thermometer. "Your eyes can't tell you how hot the oil is," he said. "This instrument can." When the oil was ready, he said, "Now proceed to the next step. Put the chicken into the flour, then carefully into the oil." Nina proceeded slowly and carefully. When each piece was golden brown, she put it on a large metal sheet to rest. Soon her sheet was full.

While the chicken was resting, Mr. Ross talked about being creative. "Once you know the basic steps, you can be creative," he said. "Add a little sugar to the flour, for example. Many great American dishes began as a creative idea in a home kitchen."

Then the students tasted each other's creations. Mr. Ross walked around the room and said something kind about every creation. Nina's chicken was a little dark in places, but it tasted wonderful. "This is a good creation," he said. "Next week, you'll be even better."

That night, Nina carried her chicken home in a box. She thought, "If I had known that cooking was so much fun, I would have taken a class years ago."

Questions:
What does the academy offer people who want to cook at home?
It offers short educational classes for them.
What did Mr. Ross say about his job?
He said his job was to educate, not only to cook.
What did Mr. Ross say about questions?
He said there were no dumb questions in his kitchen.
What was the most important instrument for frying?
It was a small kitchen thermometer.
Where did Nina put each piece of chicken when it was golden brown?
She put it on a large metal sheet to rest.
What did Nina think that night?
She thought that if she had known cooking was so much fun, she would have taken a class years ago.

lessons.title: The Diner on the Highway
lessons.summary: An army veteran turns an old gas station on a country highway into a small family diner.
lessons.text:
For 25 years, Walter Brooks served in the army. For the last 8 of those years, he was a commander in charge of more than 200 soldiers. "Being a commander taught me 2 things," he likes to say. "Plan carefully, and always feed your people well."

After he left the army, Walter moved back to the rural area where he grew up. It is a quiet part of Kansas, with farms and small towns, and the nearest city is 60 miles away. On the old highway outside his town, there was an empty gas station that had been closed for years. Walter bought it and decided to turn it into a diner.

The work took a whole year. The building was cleaned and painted, and a new kitchen was put in. Walter kept the 2 old gas pumps in front of the building. The pumps no longer work, but they were painted bright red, and now visitors take photos next to them. The interior was designed to look like a diner from 1955. The interior has red seats, a long counter and a big mirror on the wall behind the counter. When you sit at the counter, you can see the whole room in the mirror.

Walter is not the only veteran at the diner. His cook, Maria, is a veteran too. They served in the army together. The food is simple: eggs, chicken, potatoes and Maria's famous apple pie. "It's a ma-and-pa diner," Walter says. "That means a small family business. My wife, Ann, and I are the ma and pa."

The diner opened on the Fourth of July, which is Independence Day in the United States. Walter chose Independence Day for a reason. "Independence is something every veteran cares about," he said. On the first day, folks came from every farm and town along the highway. Some folks drove 50 miles just for a cup of coffee and a piece of pie. Truck drivers stopped too, because the diner is less than a mile from the main highway. Walter knows a family on almost every mile of that road. "Rural life is quiet," he said, "but nobody here is ever alone."

"In the army, I gave orders," Walter said with a smile. "Now I take orders." He looked into the mirror behind the counter, where he could see a room full of happy folks. "This is the best job I have ever had."

Questions:
What was Walter's job in the army?
He was a commander in charge of more than 200 soldiers.
What did Walter buy on the old highway?
He bought an empty gas station.
What happened to the old gas pumps?
They were painted bright red, and now visitors take photos next to them.
What is on the wall behind the counter?
There is a big mirror on the wall behind the counter.
What does a ma-and-pa diner mean?
It means a small family business.
Why did Walter open the diner on Independence Day?
He opened it on Independence Day because independence is something every veteran cares about.

lessons.title: A Week on the Coast
lessons.summary: In her diary, Kate writes about a quiet vacation in Maine and the best clam chowder she has ever eaten.
lessons.text:
Monday, August 5

My husband, Mark, and I have just arrived in a little fishing town on the coast of Maine. We came here to relax. For a whole week, we aren't going to work or look at our phones. We are going to walk, read, eat and relax.

Tuesday, August 6

This morning we climbed the hill behind the town to see the old lighthouse by the sea. The climb took an hour, and the wind was so cold that my teeth were shaking. I wish I had brought a warmer coat. From the top, we watched the fishing boats leave the port. Their shadows moved across the water in the early morning light.

Wednesday, August 7

Today we didn't have any plans, so we walked down a random street and went into a random little restaurant near the water. It was full of men from the fishing boats in their heavy yellow rain gear. The server, a friendly young woman named Emma, told us to try the clam chowder. Chowder is a white soup made largely of clams, potatoes and milk. "Some places put red tomatoes in their chowder," Emma said, "but folks here don't think that's real chowder."

"Kate, this is the best soup in Maine," Mark said, and he was right. It was the best soup I have ever eaten. It was hot and rich, and the clams were very fresh. They must have come out of the sea that morning. Emma said the men in the yellow gear had brought them in a few hours earlier.

Thursday, August 8

We went back to the same place for lunch. This time the cook came out of the kitchen to talk to us. His name is Joe, and his family has been fishing here for 4 generations. He told us the town is largely the same as it was 50 years ago. Then he wrote down his chowder recipe for us. Emma, our server, laughed. "He doesn't do that for everyone," she said.

Friday, August 9

It's our last evening. We sat on the rocks and relaxed, watching the long shadows of the boats on the water. The sea was quiet, and so were we. If we hadn't walked down that random street, we would never have found Joe's chowder. By this time next week, I will have made my first chowder at home. I will make it on a cold evening, when the wind makes my teeth shake, just like here in Maine.

Questions:
Why did Kate and Mark come to the little town?
They came there to relax.
Why were Kate's teeth shaking during the climb?
They were shaking because the wind was so cold.
How did they find the little restaurant?
They walked down a random street and went into a random little restaurant.
What were the men from the fishing boats wearing?
They were wearing heavy yellow rain gear.
What is chowder made of?
It is made largely of clams, potatoes and milk.
What will Kate have done by this time next week?
She will have made her first chowder at home.

lessons.title: The Apple Pie Auction
lessons.summary: Ten-year-old Maggie bakes an apple pie for a church auction that raises money for toys.
lessons.text:
Every November, Saint Anne's Church holds an apple pie auction. The money goes to the children's hospital in the city, and the hospital uses it to buy toys for children who have to stay there over the holidays. This year, Maggie Brennan, who is 10 years old, decided to make a pie for it.

Maggie's grandmother, Helen, is a legend in the town. She has won the apple pie contest at the county fair 15 times. "Helen's pie is a legend," people often tell Maggie. Helen helped Maggie, but she let her do all the work herself. When Maggie dropped the flour on the floor for the second time, Helen only laughed and cleaned it up. "You have the patience of a saint," Maggie told her.

First, they cut the apples and mixed them with sugar. Then Maggie rolled out the top crust and cut it into long strips. She used the strips to make the face of a lion, because the lion is her favorite animal, and the high school team is called the Lions. When the pie was ready, Maggie wrote her name on a small card. She tied the card to the box with a piece of red string and put a strip of tape on it, so it wouldn't fall off. Helen tied the string a second time, just to be safe, and added another piece of tape.

On Saturday, 30 pies in white boxes stood on a long table in the church hall. Father Michael explained the rules. "When I hold up a pie, you can bid on it," he said. "The person who makes the highest bid takes the pie home." People bid $15, $20 or $30 for most pies. When Helen's pie came up, the bidding went up to $100.

Then Father Michael held up Maggie's lion pie. Mr. Hall, who owns the shoe store, made the first bid: $20. A young woman bid $30. They kept bidding, and in the end Mr. Hall bought it for $75. "I couldn't let a lion pie go to anyone else," he said. "I played for the Lions 40 years ago."

That evening, the church counted the money. The auction had raised $2,400, enough to buy 200 toys. Holding Helen's hand, Maggie walked home, already planning next year's pie.

Questions:
Where does the money from the auction go?
It goes to the children's hospital, which uses it to buy toys for the children.
Why is Helen a legend in the town?
She is a legend because she has won the apple pie contest at the county fair 15 times.
What did Maggie make with the strips?
She made the face of a lion on top of her pie.
How did Maggie keep the card on the box?
She tied it with a piece of red string and put a strip of tape on it.
Who bought Maggie's pie, and for how much?
Mr. Hall bought it for $75.
How many toys could the church buy?
It could buy 200 toys.

lessons.title: Food and Memory
lessons.summary: A newspaper column about why the smell and taste of food bring back memories and emotions.
lessons.text:
Last Tuesday, I was walking to a doctor's appointment when I passed a small restaurant. The smell of fresh corn bread came through the open door, and for a moment I was 8 years old again, sitting in my mother's kitchen on a Sunday morning. I stood outside that door for 5 minutes and almost missed my appointment.

Why does food do this to us? Scientists say that smell is closely related to memory and emotion. The part of the brain that deals with smell is very close to the parts that deal with memory and emotion. That is why a smell can bring back a strong emotion so quickly, often before we even know what we are smelling.

I think most readers can relate to this. Ask anyone about their favorite food, and they will rarely talk about taste alone. They will talk about people and places. A friend of mine can't eat a fresh peach without thinking of her family's farm in Georgia. Another friend says a hot dog tastes like summer ball games with his father. We can all relate to stories like these.

When I was a small child, our kitchen was my whole universe. Everything important in my universe happened there. My mother cooked, and I sat on the floor with a pan and a spoon and pretended to cook too. Sometimes I pretended to be a famous cook on TV, explaining each step to my cat. My mother never told me to stop pretending. She just gave me a little flour to put in my pan.

The tone of our family meals mattered as much as the food. At our table, the tone was always warm and relaxed. We talked about our day, and nobody was in a hurry. I believe that is why simple corn bread still makes me feel safe.

It's a shame that so many families today eat in a hurry, in front of a screen, or never sit down together at all. It's a shame not because the food is worse, but because they are missing the memories that the food could carry for 50 years.

So here is my small piece of advice. Once a week, put your phone aside, set aside an hour and cook something simple with someone you love. Years from now, the smell of that dish may bring back the whole evening.

Questions:
Where was the writer going last Tuesday?
The writer was going to a doctor's appointment.
What is smell closely related to?
It is closely related to memory and emotion.
What did the writer pretend to be as a child?
The writer pretended to be a famous cook on TV.
What was the tone of the family meals?
The tone was always warm and relaxed.
Why does the writer think it is a shame that families eat in a hurry?
It is a shame because they are missing the memories that the food could carry.
What is the writer's advice?
Once a week, put your phone aside and cook something simple with someone you love.

lessons.title: Cooking on the Radio
lessons.summary: A jazz singer in New Orleans is chosen to host a new radio show that mixes cooking and music.
lessons.text:
For 30 years, Della Johnson has been singing jazz in the clubs of New Orleans. She is one of the best-known singers in the city. But Della has another love: cooking. Every Sunday, she cooks for her friends, and she is always singing in the kitchen while she cooks.

Last spring, the city's public radio station was looking for a host for a new weekend show. The station wanted a show about the food and music of New Orleans. After meeting several people, the station appointed Della as the host. "When they told me I had been appointed, I couldn't believe it," she said. "I'm a singer, not a radio host."

The station's director, Paul Martin, explained the format of the new show. "The format is simple," he said. "For an hour, Della cooks a dish from New Orleans in our studio kitchen and explains every step. While the food is cooking, she talks about the history of the dish, and between the steps, a band plays live music. At the end, Della does some singing herself." Each show is broadcast live on Saturday morning, and it is broadcast again on Sunday evening for people who missed it.

The show is not only entertainment. Mr. Martin wanted it to engage listeners and teach them something. "Good entertainment can also teach," he said. "We want to engage our listeners, not just talk to them." Listeners can call the show and ask questions, and every week, Della reads a family recipe that a listener has sent in.

The first show was broadcast in June. Della cooked red beans and rice, a typical Monday dish in New Orleans, and a well-known singer from the city sang with her at the end. The phone did not stop ringing for the whole hour. Hundreds of listeners called to ask questions or share their own memories of red beans and rice.

The show has been a big success. "This time next year, we'll still be cooking and singing on Saturday mornings," Della said. "And I'll still be learning from our listeners. They know more about cooking than I do!"

Questions:
What has Della been doing for 30 years?
She has been singing jazz in the clubs of New Orleans.
Who was appointed as the host?
Della was appointed as the host.
What is the format of the show?
Della cooks a dish and explains every step, a band plays live music, and at the end she does some singing.
When is the show broadcast?
It is broadcast live on Saturday morning and again on Sunday evening.
How does the show engage its listeners?
Listeners can call and ask questions, and Della reads recipes that listeners send in.
What did Della cook on the first show?
She cooked red beans and rice.

lessons.title: A Restaurant Comes Back
lessons.summary: A short news report on how a family restaurant reopened a year after a hurricane destroyed it.
lessons.text:
PORT LOUIS, Louisiana — A year after a hurricane destroyed much of this small fishing town, one of its oldest restaurants opened its doors again on Saturday.

Marie's Place has served gumbo, fried fish and rice to the people of Port Louis since 1962. The establishment was started by Marie Broussard and is now run by her grandson, Paul. For 60 years, the family has succeeded in keeping the same simple food and the same low prices. Last September, the hurricane destroyed the restaurant's roof and kitchen, and the dining room was under 3 feet of water. "When I saw it, I was sure it was the end," Paul Broussard said. "I didn't think we could succeed in opening again."

For months, the restaurant was unable to open. Paul and his staff were unable to work, and many of them had also lost their homes. The town's recovery was slow. Roads, schools and houses had to be rebuilt first.

The restaurant had to rely on help from many people. The state gave financial assistance to small businesses that had been destroyed, and Marie's Place received some of that assistance. A kitchen equipment manufacturer from Texas gave the restaurant 2 new ovens for free. "The manufacturer called us and asked what we needed," Mr. Broussard said. "We didn't even ask them." Volunteers from all over the country helped to clean and paint the building.

While the restaurant was closed, Mr. Broussard did not stop cooking. He moved his work to a church kitchen, a large facility with space for 10 cooks. In that facility, he and his staff cooked free meals for families who had lost their homes. They worked with a local food bank that tries to combat hunger in the area. "After a storm, you have to combat hunger first," Mr. Broussard said. "People can rely on a hot meal, even when nothing else is certain."

On Saturday, more than 300 people waited outside the restaurant before it opened. Many of them had been coming to the establishment for 40 years. "If people hadn't helped us, we would never have opened again," Mr. Broussard said. "This recovery belongs to the whole town."

Questions:
What happened to Marie's Place last September?
The hurricane destroyed its roof and kitchen, and the dining room was under water.
Who runs the establishment now?
Marie's grandson, Paul Broussard, runs it now.
Why was the town's recovery slow?
It was slow because roads, schools and houses had to be rebuilt first.
What did the manufacturer from Texas give the restaurant?
It gave the restaurant 2 new ovens for free.
What did Mr. Broussard do while the restaurant was closed?
He cooked free meals for families in a church kitchen and worked with a food bank to combat hunger.
How many people waited outside on Saturday?
More than 300 people waited outside.
